accepted.s: The National Green Tribunal was established under which of the following enactments?
o: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
accepted.x: The National Green Tribunal was set up under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
accepted.tq: Test the exact parent legislation rather than the subject area of the tribunal.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the constitutional status and powers of the National Green Tribunal?
o: It is a statutory body with powers similar to those of a civil court.
It is a constitutional body with powers exclusively of an administrative authority.
It is an executive body exercising only advisory jurisdiction.
It is a constitutional body established under Article 323B without civil-court powers.
accepted.x: The NGT is a statutory, not constitutional, body and possesses civil-court powers in matters within its jurisdiction.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between constitutional, statutory and executive bodies before considering their powers.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s:
With reference to the procedure followed by the National Green Tribunal, consider the following statements:
1. It is bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
2. It is guided by the principles of natural justice.
3. It is required to dispose of applications within six months.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The NGT is not bound by the CPC, 1908; it follows natural justice and applications are to be disposed of within six months.
accepted.tq: Identify the reversed procedural claim and combine the two correct procedural features.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s:
Which of the following principles are applied by the National Green Tribunal?
1. Sustainable development
2. Precautionary principle
3. Polluter pays principle
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: The NGT applies all three principles: sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
accepted.tq: Use the complete principle-list option when every listed environmental principle belongs to the tribunal’s framework.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: The establishment of the National Green Tribunal gives effect, in the environmental context, to which Fundamental Right?
o: Right to constitutional remedies under Article 32
accepted.x: The NGT gives effect to the right to a healthy environment, which is treated as part of the right to life under Article 21.
accepted.tq: Match the environmental entitlement with the relevant Fundamental Right.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: The Principal Bench of the National Green Tribunal is located at:
accepted.x: New Delhi is the location of the Principal Bench of the NGT.
accepted.tq: Test the headquarters-type location separately from zonal and circuit bench locations.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Type of Bench)
 a. Principal Bench
 b. Zonal Bench
 c. Circuit Bench

List-II (Place)
 i. Jodhpur
 ii. New Delhi
 iii. Pune
 iv. Shillong
accepted.x: The Principal Bench is at New Delhi; Pune is a zonal bench location; and Jodhpur and Shillong are circuit bench locations.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure Principal Bench pair and then distinguish zonal from circuit locations.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT a location of a zonal bench of the National Green Tribunal?
accepted.x: Pune, Bhopal and Chennai are zonal bench locations. Shillong is a circuit bench location.
accepted.tq: Find the bench-type mismatch rather than merely identifying a place associated with the NGT.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: The National Green Tribunal is headed by a Chairperson who is required to be:
o: The Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
A retired member of the Union Public Service Commission
A serving judge of a High Court
A retired judge of the Supreme Court
accepted.x: The NGT is headed by a Chairperson who is a retired Supreme Court judge, assisted by judicial and expert members.
accepted.tq: Apply the who-holds-the-office test to distinguish judicial leadership from executive administration.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: The National Green Tribunal is best described as a specialised and multidisciplinary body for:
o: Environmental protection, forest and natural-resource conservation, environmental legal rights, and relief for damage
Exclusively regulating wildlife sanctuaries and national parks
Adjudicating all criminal offences relating to public health
Only adjudicating disputes between the Union and the States
accepted.x: Its purpose includes environmental protection, conservation of forests and natural resources, enforcement of environmental legal rights, and relief and compensation for damage.
accepted.tq: Select the option that combines the tribunal’s connected functions without extending its jurisdiction beyond the stated scope.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: Which of the following enactments falls outside the direct scope of the National Green Tribunal as stated?
o: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
accepted.x: The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 is outside the NGT’s direct scope. The Air Act, Forest Conservation Act and Biological Diversity Act are covered enactments.
accepted.tq: Look for the excluded enactment among statutes that otherwise belong to environmental law.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s:
Which of the following pairs of enactments is correctly matched with the direct scope of the National Green Tribunal?
1. Water Act, 1974
2. Air Act, 1981
3. Environment Protection Act, 1986
4. Forest Conservation Act, 1980
5. Biological Diversity Act, 2002
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: All five listed enactments fall within the direct scope of the NGT.
accepted.tq: Check the completeness of a statutory list and avoid excluding a genuine environmental enactment.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: An appeal against an order of the National Green Tribunal lies to the Supreme Court within:
accepted.x: An appeal against an NGT order may be filed before the Supreme Court within 90 days.
accepted.tq: Use the exact statutory time limit and compare the middle numerical options carefully.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs of environmental matters was associated with cases before the National Green Tribunal in 2026?
o: Silent Valley and Chilika lagoon only
Kaziranga tourism and Gir lion conservation only
Sardar Sarovar and Tehri dam rehabilitation
accepted.x: The 2026 cases identified include the Dhanauri wetland, Ganga pollution and the Saparnika river.
accepted.tq: Test current case names as a precise identification question rather than inferring from general environmental themes.
accepted.sec: National Green Tribunal - Act, principles, benches, CPC

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 323A:
1. It concerns recruitment and conditions of service of public servants.
2. It may cover employees of the Centre, States, local bodies and public sector undertakings.
3. Tribunals under it may be established by Parliament only.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Article 323A covers recruitment and service conditions of public servants across the listed levels and permits Parliament alone to establish such tribunals.
accepted.tq: Separate the subject jurisdiction from the law-making authority and retain all three supported statements.
accepted.sec: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

accepted.s: Which one of the following subjects is associated with Article 323B but NOT with Article 323A?
o: Service conditions in public sector undertakings
Conditions of service of State employees
accepted.x: Land reforms are among the subjects listed under Article 323B. Article 323A deals with recruitment and service conditions of public servants.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the service-matter jurisdiction of Article 323A and the broader subject list of Article 323B.
accepted.sec: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

accepted.s:
Which of the following subjects is covered under Article 323B?
1. Taxation
2. Foreign exchange
3. Industrial and labour disputes
4. Elections
5. Rent and tenancy
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: Article 323B includes taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, elections, rent and tenancy, along with other specified subjects.
accepted.tq: Treat the listed subjects as a broad statutory-tribunal field and verify each item before selecting the complete code.
accepted.sec: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

accepted.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes the authorities competent to establish tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B?
o: The President establishes tribunals under Article 323A and the Governor under Article 323B.
Only State legislatures may establish tribunals under both Articles.
Parliament and State legislatures may establish tribunals under Article 323A, whereas only Parliament may do so under Article 323B.
Parliament alone may establish tribunals under Article 323A, whereas Parliament and State legislatures may do so under Article 323B within their competence.
accepted.x: Article 323A permits Parliament alone to establish tribunals for service matters. Under Article 323B, Parliament and State legislatures may establish tribunals within their respective legislative competence.
accepted.tq: Ask who would do this job and compare the constitutional authority under the two Articles.
accepted.sec: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

accepted.s:
With reference to the structure of tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B, consider the following statements:
1. Article 323A contemplates one tribunal for the Centre and one for each State or group of States.
2. Article 323A permits a hierarchy of original and appellate tribunals.
3. A hierarchy of tribunals is allowed under Article 323B.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Article 323A contemplates one tribunal for the Centre and one for each State or group of States, without a hierarchy. Article 323B allows a hierarchy, including original and appellate tribunals.
accepted.tq: Spot the reversed structural feature: the hierarchy belongs to Article 323B, not Article 323A.
accepted.sec: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

accepted.s: Articles 323A and 323B were inserted in the Constitution by which Amendment?
accepted.x: Both Articles were inserted as Part XIV-A by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the amendment that inserted the Articles from the later amendment that added a subject clause.
accepted.sec: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

accepted.s: Rent and tenancy were added as a subject under Article 323B by the:
accepted.x: The rent and tenancy clause, clause (h), was added to Article 323B by the 75th Constitutional Amendment, 1993.
accepted.tq: Separate the original insertion amendment from the later amendment that expanded the subject list.
accepted.sec: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

accepted.s: The insertion of Articles 323A and 323B into Part XIV-A was associated with the recommendations of which committee?
accepted.x: The insertion of Articles 323A and 323B by the 42nd Amendment is associated with the Swaran Singh Committee.
accepted.tq: Match the constitutional reform recommendation with the correct committee name.
accepted.sec: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

accepted.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Rojer Mathew
B. L. Chandra Kumar
C. R. Gandhi
D. S.P. Sampath Kumar
accepted.x: The correct sequence is S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987), L. Chandra Kumar (1997), R. Gandhi (2010), and Rojer Mathew (2019).
accepted.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intervening decisions by year.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

accepted.s: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Tribunals completely replace the jurisdiction of High Courts.
Only the President may review decisions of tribunals.
Judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is part of the basic structure and tribunal decisions are subject to review by a High Court Division Bench.
Article 323A is unconstitutional in its entirety.
accepted.x: L. Chandra Kumar held that judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is part of the basic structure. Tribunal decisions can therefore be reviewed by a High Court Division Bench; tribunals supplement rather than replace High Courts.
accepted.tq: Identify the precise holding instead of accepting the extreme claim that tribunals replace High Courts.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

accepted.s: Which of the following constitutional provisions were struck down in L. Chandra Kumar as exclusion clauses?
accepted.x: The Supreme Court struck down the exclusion clauses contained in Article 323A(2)(d) and Article 323B(3)(d).
accepted.tq: Check both the Article numbers and their sub-clauses, since a nearby provision is a likely trap.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

accepted.s:
Assertion (A): Tribunals supplement the High Courts but do not replace them.
Reason (R): Judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
accepted.x: Both statements are true, and the basic-structure status of judicial review explains why tribunals cannot replace the constitutional review jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court.
accepted.tq: Test whether the constitutional principle in the Reason directly explains the institutional conclusion in the Assertion.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

accepted.s: Which case preceded L. Chandra Kumar in the development of the law relating to tribunal review?
accepted.x: S.P. Sampath Kumar was decided in 1987, before L. Chandra Kumar in 1997.
accepted.tq: Use the case timeline to identify the immediately preceding authority.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

accepted.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Rojer Mathew — 2010 — members independent of the executive
S.P. Sampath Kumar — 2019 — National Tribunals Commission
L. Chandra Kumar — 1997 — exclusion clauses struck down
R. Gandhi — 1987 — tribunals may replace High Courts
accepted.x: L. Chandra Kumar was decided in 1997 and struck down the exclusion clauses. S.P. Sampath Kumar was decided in 1987, R. Gandhi in 2010, and Rojer Mathew in 2019.
accepted.tq: Verify the year and holding together; wrong options commonly pair a correct case with another case’s holding.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

accepted.s: In R. Gandhi (2010), the Supreme Court emphasised that:
o: Tribunal members must be independent of the executive.
Only State legislatures may establish tribunals.
All tribunal decisions are final and unreviewable.
Tribunals must have no judicial members.
accepted.x: R. Gandhi emphasised the need for tribunal members to be independent of the executive.
accepted.tq: Match the case with its institutional-independence holding rather than with the later review doctrine.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

accepted.s: Rojer Mathew (2019) is associated with the recommendation for establishing an independent:
accepted.x: Rojer Mathew recommended an independent National Tribunals Commission.
accepted.tq: Distinguish similarly named national bodies and select the institution specifically connected with tribunal administration.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

accepted.s: The Madras Bar Association decisions of 2021 and November 2025 were concerned with provisions that:
o: Inserted Articles 323A and 323B into the Constitution
Transferred all environmental cases to the National Green Tribunal
Re-enacted conditions previously rejected by the Court in relation to tribunals
Abolished judicial review under Articles 32 and 226
accepted.x: The Madras Bar Association decisions struck down Tribunal Reforms provisions that re-enacted conditions previously rejected by the Court.
accepted.tq: Identify the later case by its specific tribunal-reform issue rather than by the broader theme of judicial review.
accepted.sec: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions
